metadata.title: Optical and magnetic microrobotics
metadata.description: Illustrated research projects in optical manipulation, microscopy perception, magnetic navigation, shared autonomy and reconfigurable miniature robots.

hero.title: Optical and magnetic microrobotics
hero.lead: We design, observe and control small robots using light and magnetic fields. Our research connects physical embodiment, microscopy, learning and human interaction to make precise manipulation possible across different scales and environments.

introduction.title: From a fabricated body to a useful manipulation capability
introduction.text: A small robot’s motion depends on its geometry, the surrounding medium, the available field and what can be observed. We study these elements together: how to create controllable structures, infer their state from images, learn with limited data and decide how a human or controller should act.
introduction.note: The projects below span optical microrobots, magnetic microrobots and related millirobot systems. Each project identifies its scale and evaluation setting; simulation, phantom experiments and physical manipulation answer different questions.

groups.title: Optical manipulation and digital twins
groups.description: From distributed laser forces to interactive simulation: how robot geometry, trapping and feedback produce controlled motion.

projects.name: Distributed optical-force control
projects.title: Distributed force control for microrobot manipulation via planar multi‐spot optical tweezer
projects.question: How can planar laser traps control motion outside the microscope image plane?
projects.approach: Fabricated microrobot geometries convert forces from multiple optical traps into translation and rotation. Adjusting trap spacing and the distribution of laser power changes the force and torque balance.
projects.evidence: The study compares fabricated designs and demonstrates out-of-plane control and indirect manipulation of micro-objects using planar multi-spot optical tweezers.
projects.scope: Capabilities depend on robot geometry, trap configuration and the experimental medium.

figure.alt: Original concept figure showing planar laser spots, the microrobot rotation mechanism and six microrobot geometries.
figure.caption: Physical mechanism and microrobot design for out-of-plane optical control, Figure 1.
figure.credit: Zhang et al. (2020), published by Wiley-VCH; Figure 1 extracted and resized.
figure.title: Distributed optical-force control

projects.name: Interactive OT Gym
projects.title: Interactive OT Gym: A Reinforcement Learning-Based Interactive Optical tweezer (OT)-Driven Microrobotics Simulation Platform
projects.question: How can operators and learned policies cooperate in optical micromanipulation?
projects.approach: The simulation platform combines optical-field modelling, reinforcement learning, haptic interaction and context-dependent shared control for cooperative manipulation.
projects.evidence: The reported simulated cell-manipulation task achieved approximately 67% shorter completion time and 100% success under shared control, relative to the tested human-only and RL-only conditions.
projects.scope: These figures describe the study’s simulator and task protocol, not a clinical or general-purpose success rate.

figure.alt: A project overview illustrates an optical-tweezer simulation, reinforcement learning and haptic human-robot interaction.
figure.caption: Author project figure — the Interactive OT Gym platform.
figure.title: Interactive OT Gym
figure.credit: Zongcai Tan, Dandan Zhang (2025).

projects.name: Visuo-haptic optical digital twin
projects.title: A Digital Twin Framework for Virtual Visuo-Haptic Teleoperation of Complex-Shaped Optical Microrobots
projects.question: How can an operator feel interaction and trap stability in a virtual optical-microrobot task?
projects.approach: A ROS-connected bimanual interface links microscopy-based pose/depth estimation, microrobot motion simulation and model-based force rendering. Distributed manipulation modelling is combined with optical-force estimates.
projects.evidence: In simulated cell delivery, success increased from 30% to 80%. The standard deviations of contact-force and trap-centre-distance metrics fell by 53.2% and 55.2%, respectively.
projects.scope: Haptic cues are model-derived. These results establish virtual-task performance and consistency with the fitted model.

figure.alt: A digital-twin framework links the haptic user interface, microscopy-based pose estimation, robot simulation and optical-force rendering.
figure.caption: Author project figure — visuo-haptic optical microrobot teleoperation.
figure.title: Visuo-haptic optical digital twin
figure.credit: Zongcai Tan, Lan Wei, Dandan Zhang (2026).

groups.title: Microscopy, datasets and learning
groups.description: Depth and out-of-plane orientation change an object’s appearance. These studies connect physical imaging cues, data-efficient learning and reproducible evaluation.

projects.name: Microscopic pose and depth estimation
projects.title: Data-driven microscopic pose and depth estimation for optical microrobot manipulation
projects.question: What can a single microscope view reveal about three-dimensional microrobot state?
projects.approach: Image detection and a residual network estimate pose, while focus-derived features support Gaussian-process depth regression. Temporal filtering helps integrate estimates across observations.
projects.evidence: The work connects image appearance, robot orientation and depth through a calibrated perception pipeline for optical manipulation.
projects.scope: Pose-dependent imaging and calibration remain part of the measurement model; estimates are not direct force measurements.

figure.alt: Original processing diagram combining image detection, a residual neural network, Gaussian-process regression and a Kalman filter for microrobot pose and depth.
figure.caption: GPR–ResNet pose and depth estimation with few-shot calibration, Figure 5.
figure.credit: Zhang et al. (2020), © American Chemical Society; Figure 5 from the accepted manuscript, extracted and resized.
figure.title: Microscopic pose and depth estimation

projects.name: Sim-to-real learning with small datasets
projects.title: Micro-object pose estimation with sim-to-real transfer learning using small dataset
projects.question: Can pose estimation work with limited labelled microscopy data?
projects.approach: Image translation narrows the simulation-to-experiment appearance gap. A learning-to-match embedding aligns samples with the same pose before a compact predictor estimates orientation.
projects.evidence: The study evaluates data-efficient pose learning for optical- and electron-microscope observations, including poses absent from the collected training examples.
projects.scope: The paper provides code and data on request. The later public sim-to-real repository is a separate release.

figure.alt: Original figure showing generated and microscope images with a shared feature-embedding model for microrobot pose estimation.
figure.caption: Sim-to-real learning-to-match model, Figure 3.
figure.credit: Zhang et al. (2022); Figure 3 extracted from the publisher PDF and resized.
figure.title: Sim-to-real learning with small datasets

projects.name: OTMR: an optical-microrobot benchmark
projects.title: A Dataset and Benchmarks for Deep Learning-Based Optical Microrobot Pose and Depth Perception
projects.question: How can microscopy perception methods be compared on a shared dataset?
projects.approach: OTMR pairs diverse microrobot geometries with microscopy observations and benchmarks pose classification and depth regression across eight deep-learning architectures.
projects.evidence: The dataset contains 232,881 images, 18 microrobot types and 176 distinct poses. The study also examines how training-set size affects performance.
projects.scope: Preserve the released label definitions and split protocol when comparing models.

figure.alt: A grid pairs CAD models and microscope images of different optical microrobot geometries.
figure.caption: Author project figure — optical microrobot geometries and observations.
figure.title: OTMR: an optical-microrobot benchmark
figure.credit: Lan Wei, Dandan Zhang (2025).

projects.name: Physics-informed sim-to-real augmentation
projects.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Efficient Sim-to-Real Data Augmentation in Micro-Object Pose Estimation
projects.question: How can synthetic images retain depth-dependent optical appearance?
projects.approach: Wave-optics rendering and depth alignment provide physically informed inputs to GAN-based image translation, producing labelled microscopy-like images for pose training.
projects.evidence: The paper reports 35.6% higher SSIM than the compared AI-only approach and CNN pitch/roll accuracies of 93.9%/91.9% when trained on synthetic images.
projects.scope: Comparisons use the paper’s image-generation and pose-estimation protocols; public code and local optical parameters require configuration.

figure.alt: A pipeline connects microrobot CAD models, physics-based image rendering, image translation and pose estimation.
figure.caption: Author project figure — physics-informed sim-to-real pose estimation.
figure.title: Physics-informed sim-to-real augmentation
figure.credit: Zongcai Tan, Lan Wei, Dandan Zhang (2026).

projects.name: Adaptive-grid depth estimation
projects.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning with Adaptive Grids for Optical Microrobot Depth Estimation
projects.question: Can physical focus cues make depth learning more data-efficient?
projects.approach: CNN features are combined with focus measures such as image entropy, gradients and Laplacian responses. Finer grids cover the robot, while coarser grids cover background.
projects.evidence: The reported experiments reduce depth MSE by more than 60% against the evaluated baselines. With 20% of the data, the method outperformed a ResNet50 trained on the full dataset.
projects.scope: These are study-specific comparisons across the tested microrobot types; preprocessing and depth-label alignment matter.

figure.alt: Rows compare microscopy views and CAD side views of optical microrobots at different focal depths.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 2 — microrobot appearance across focal depths.
figure.title: Adaptive-grid depth estimation
figure.credit: Lan Wei, Lou Genoud, Dandan Zhang (2025).

projects.name: Du-FreqNet: depth-conditioned microscopy
projects.title: Dual-Control Frequency-Aware Diffusion Model for Depth-Dependent Optical Microrobot Microscopy Image Generation
projects.question: How can image generation reproduce both geometry and defocus patterns?
projects.approach: Two ControlNet branches encode three-dimensional point clouds and depth-specific mesh information. An adaptive Fourier-domain loss changes the frequency emphasis with distance from focus.
projects.evidence: The preprint reports controllable depth-dependent synthesis, 20.7% higher SSIM than its baselines and benefits for downstream pose/depth estimation, including unseen poses.
projects.scope: This is a preprint result. Image similarity and downstream estimation are distinct evaluation objectives.

figure.alt: A diffusion-model architecture uses geometric conditions, dual control branches and frequency-domain supervision.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 2 — depth-conditioned microscopy image generation.
figure.title: Du-FreqNet: depth-conditioned microscopy
figure.credit: Lan Wei, Zongcai Tan, Kangyi Lu, Jian-Qing Zheng, Dandan Zhang (2026).

groups.title: Magnetic intelligence and reconfiguration
groups.description: Magnetic fields support contactless actuation. We investigate navigation, bimanual coordination, task-dependent assistance and the capabilities gained by changing the actuator or robot configuration.

projects.name: Immersive magnetic navigation
projects.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Semi-Autonomous Control for Magnetic Micro-robot Navigation with Immersive Manipulation
projects.question: How can human judgement and learned navigation share control in constrained channels?
projects.approach: A deep-RL controller is combined with mixed-reality manual interaction. The immersive view helps the operator interpret the environment and coordinate assistance.
projects.evidence: The study evaluates navigation efficiency, control error and robustness in simulated microvascular environments, comparing shared control with the tested alternatives.
projects.scope: Simulated microvascular navigation does not establish in-vivo performance.

figure.alt: A magnetic microrobot navigation diagram combines immersive manual interaction with reinforcement-learning-based autonomous control.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 1 — immersive semi-autonomous magnetic navigation.
figure.title: Immersive magnetic navigation
figure.credit: Yudong Mao, Dandan Zhang (2025).

projects.name: Bi-CAST: bimanual shared control
projects.title: Context-Aware Adaptive Shared Control for Magnetically-Driven Bimanual Dexterous Micromanipulation
projects.question: How should two magnetic actuators share control with a human operator?
projects.approach: Visual history, spatial risk and task state adjust each manipulator’s authority continuously. Bidirectional haptics combines operator-intent recognition with risk-dependent guidance.
projects.evidence: Eight participants completed three vascular-phantom tasks. Against the reported baselines, the best reductions reached 76.6% in collisions and 44.4% in NASA-TLX workload; trajectory smoothness improved by 25.9%.
projects.scope: The preprint reports a phantom user study. “Up to” improvements depend on the comparison and task.

figure.alt: A shared-control diagram connects human haptic input, path planning, task observations and bimanual magnetic micromanipulation.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 1 — context-aware bimanual shared control.
figure.title: Bi-CAST: bimanual shared control
figure.credit: Yongchen Wang, Kangyi Lu, Lan Wei, Dandan Zhang (2026).

projects.name: Mag-VLA: language-guided magnetic manipulation
projects.title: Mag-VLA: Vision-Language-Action Model for Bimanual Magnetically Actuated Microrobot Manipulation
projects.question: Can visual observations and language organise a multi-stage magnetic manipulation task?
projects.approach: A vision–language backbone is adapted for coordinated two-arm actuation. A phase classifier and an Action Chunking Transformer decoder organise approach and transport trajectories.
projects.evidence: Physical-robot experiments report 90% approach success across three task configurations. Transport success was 80%, 70% and 50% as task difficulty increased.
projects.scope: Approach and transport are separate outcomes; the result does not imply 90% end-to-end task success.

figure.alt: A microscope observes magnetically actuated microrobots controlled by two micromanipulators, with approach and transport phases.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 1 — Mag-VLA setup and manipulation pipeline.
figure.title: Mag-VLA: language-guided magnetic manipulation
figure.credit: Yongchen Wang, Kangyi Lu, Lan Wei, Dandan Zhang (2026).

projects.name: DexterousMag: reconfiguring the actuator
projects.title: DexterousMag: A Reconfigurable Electromagnetic Actuation System for Miniature Helical Robot
projects.question: When should the field-generating hardware change its geometry?
projects.approach: A robot-arm-assisted three-coil system adjusts its polar angle. Finite-element field and gradient libraries expose the trade-off between deeper reach and stronger near-surface capability.
projects.evidence: The preprint evaluates deep translation, planar tracking and three-dimensional lifting, and compares online geometry scheduling with fixed configurations.
projects.scope: This study reconfigures the external actuation system; it is distinct from changing the miniature robot’s body.

figure.alt: A robot-arm-mounted electromagnetic actuation system changes coil-group geometry around a miniature helical robot.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 1 — the reconfigurable DexterousMag actuation concept.
figure.title: DexterousMag: reconfiguring the actuator
figure.credit: Jialin Lin, Dandan Zhang (2026).

projects.name: Modular magnetic millirobots
projects.title: Design and Control of Modular Magnetic Millirobots for Multimodal Locomotion and Shape Reconfiguration
projects.question: Can small magnetic modules assemble into shapes suited to different tasks?
projects.approach: Free, fixed and gripper modules combine uniform and gradient field inputs for navigation, flip-and-walk motion, assembly and cargo handling. Visual feedback and A* planning support navigation.
projects.evidence: Chain-to-gripper transformations succeeded in 90% of reported trials; chain-to-square changes were less consistent, exposing a dependence on module geometry.
projects.scope: These are millimetre-scale modules. Their reliability and actuation conditions should not be extrapolated directly to micrometre-scale robots.

figure.alt: Modular magnetic millirobot geometries and a diagram of navigation, self-assembly and shape reconfiguration.
figure.caption: Author-manuscript Fig. 1 — modular magnetic millirobot design and behaviours.
figure.title: Modular magnetic millirobots
figure.credit: Erik Garcia Oyono, Jialin Lin, Dandan Zhang (2026).

fabrication.title: Rapid, parallel fabrication of magnetic robot bodies
fabrication.paperTitle: Rapid Parallel Fabrication and Control of Diverse Microrobotic Structures with Magnetic Functionalization
fabrication.description: The Magni-DOME platform combines projection-based photolithography with magnetic patterning to fabricate and characterise magnetically functionalised hydrogel structures in one setup. The study demonstrates parallel production of different shapes and sizes and examines the behaviour of selected designs.
fabrication.scope: This is a fabrication-and-actuation contribution; it does not establish a single optimal body for every manipulation task.

outlook.title: Measure the limits of a configuration
outlook.text: Map which motions and interactions a robot–actuator combination can reliably produce, and how those capabilities change with geometry, depth and environment.

outlook.title: Connect prediction to physical evidence
outlook.text: Use new observations to check image models and digital twins, including where a model becomes uncertain or fails to transfer.

outlook.title: Decide when adaptation is enough
outlook.text: Compare controller adaptation with physical reconfiguration under matched tasks, including the time and reliability costs of changing shape or actuation geometry.
